तदेतत्सर्वेभ्योऽङ्गेभ्यस्तेजः सम्भूतमात्मन्येवात्मानं बिभर्ति ।
तद्यदा स्त्रियां सिञ्चत्यथैनज्जनयति ।
तदस्य प्रथमं जन्म ॥ १ ॥

padaccheda.deva: पुरुषे ह वै अयम् आदितः गर्भः भवति यत् एतत् रेतः तत् एतत् सर्वेभ्यः अङ्गेभ्यः तेजः सम्भूतम् आत्मनि एव आत्मानम् बिभर्ति तत् यदा स्त्रियाम् सिञ्चति अथ एनत् जनयति तत् अस्य प्रथमम् जन्म

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. sg.

translations.text: In a man, indeed, this one (the transmigrating self) first becomes an embryo: that which is this seed. This, the vigour gathered from all the limbs, he bears as a self in himself. When he pours it into a woman, then he begets it. That is its first birth.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the adhyāya: the meaning of the adhyāya just ended is this. He who makes the origin, continuance and dissolution of the world, who is not in saṃsāra, all-knowing and all-powerful, created this whole world in the order beginning with space without taking any thing other than himself, and himself entered all the bodies that have prāṇa in order to awaken to his own Self; and having entered he awoke directly to his own Self as it is: ‘I am this Brahman’. Therefore he alone is the one Self in all bodies, and there is no other; and another too should know ‘he is my Self, I am Brahman’. It may be objected: for the all-pervading Self of all there is nothing, not so much as the tip of a hair, that he has not entered; how then did he cleave the parting and enter, like an ant into a hole? But this is a very small objection, and much more could be objected: that without organs he reflected; that without material he created the worlds; that he drew a Puruṣa out of the waters and gave it shape; that from his brooding the mouth and the rest burst forth, and from them fire and the other guardians; their being joined with hunger and thirst, their asking for an abode, the showing of the cow and the rest, their entering each its abode, the flight of the food, the wish to seize it with speech and the rest: all this is on a level with the cleaving of the parting and the entry. Let it all be unfitting, then? No: only the awakening to the Self is meant here, so all this is explanatory statement (arthavāda), and there is no fault. Or the god of great māyā, all-knowing and all-powerful, did all this as a magician would. The more fitting view is that the elaboration of stories is, as in the world, for ease of understanding; for no fruit is held to come from knowing the story of creation, but immortality is the fruit, known in all the Upaniṣads and in the smṛtis (Gītā 13.27), of knowing the oneness of the Self.

Śaṅkara, introducing the adhyāya, the objection: there are three selves. One is the jīva, the enjoyer and agent, who transmigrates, known to all the world and to scripture. A second conscious self, the Lord, all-knowing, the maker of the world, is inferred from the making of worlds and bodies with their many seats fit for the experience of the fruits of the actions of many creatures, as a carpenter is from the making of a city or a palace. The third is the Puruṣa of the Upaniṣads, ‘from whom words turn back’ (Taittirīya 2.4.1), ‘not this, not this’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.26). These three being unlike one another, how can it be known that there is one Self only, without a second, not transmigrating? And how is even the jīva known? As hearer, thinker, seer, commander, proclaimer, knower. But that is contradictory: he is the unthought thinker, the unknown knower, and ‘you cannot think the thinker of thought’ (3.4.2). It would be contradictory if he were known by perception, like pleasure; but perception of him is denied, and he is known by the mark of hearing and the rest. How even by a mark? While the self hears a sound it is occupied with the act of hearing alone, so that acts of thinking and knowing, about itself or anything else, are not possible; so too in thinking. And hearing and the rest act only on their own objects: the thinker's thinking is not possible on anything but what is to be thought. Everything can be thought by the mind? True, but nothing can be thought without a thinker; so the thinker of all is thinker only and cannot be what is thought, and there is no second thinker of the thinker. If he were thought by himself, there would be two, the self by which and the self which is thought, or one self split in two like a bamboo; either way it does not hold, as of two lamps one cannot be the lighter and the other the lit, being alike. Nor has the thinker any time free from thinking the thinkable in which to think the self. And if he thinks the self by a mark, the same two faults follow.

Śaṅkara, introducing the adhyāya, the reply: if he is known neither by perception nor by inference, how is it said ‘let him know: he is my Self’ (Kauṣītaki 3.9), and how ‘hearer, thinker’? It may be said that the self has the properties of hearing and the rest and also their absence, by turns: when it hears it does not think, as Devadatta when he walks does not stand; so the followers of Kaṇāda and others hold that knowledge is born of conjunction and is not simultaneous (‘my mind was elsewhere, I did not see’; the non-arising of cognitions together is the mark of the mind). But then the sense of the śruti does not hold, for hearing and the rest are accepted as eternal: ‘there is no loss of the hearing of the hearer’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.27). Nor does it follow that cognitions arise together, against experience, or that the self has no ignorance. The seeing of the eye and the other organs, which are non-eternal, have form, and are subject to conjunction and disjunction, is non-eternal, like the blazing of fire that is born of contact with grass; but the eternal, formless Self, not subject to conjunction and disjunction, cannot have a non-eternal seeing born of conjunction: ‘there is no loss of the seeing of the seer’ (4.3.23). So there are two seeings, the non-eternal one of the eye and the eternal one of the Self; and likewise two hearings, two thinkings, two knowings, outer and inner; and thus the text ‘the seer of seeing, the hearer of hearing’ fits. In the world too the seeing of the eye is known to be non-eternal, lost and gained as the darkening of the eye comes and goes, and the eternity of the Self's seeing is known: one whose eyes have been taken out says ‘today I saw my brother in a dream’, and a deaf man ‘today I heard a mantra in a dream’. If the Self's seeing were born of contact with the eye it would perish with it, and he would not see blue or yellow in a dream. The Self's eternal seeing is what grasps the outer, non-eternal seeing; because the outer seeing arises and passes away, people mistake the Self's seeing that grasps it for non-eternal too, as the sight that follows a whirling firebrand seems itself to whirl: ‘it thinks as it were, it moves as it were’ (4.3.7). Since the Self's seeing is eternal, it is neither simultaneous nor successive. The error of the world and of the logicians, who lack the tradition of scripture, that the Self's seeing is non-eternal comes from the adjunct of the outer seeing; and the imagining of a difference between jīva, Lord and supreme Self has this same cause.

Śaṅkara, introducing the adhyāya, the conclusion: he who wishes to imagine, in that nature which no word or idea reaches, in which all the distinctions of speech and mind become one, ‘it is, it is not; one, many; with qualities, without; it knows, it knows not; active, inactive; with fruit, without; with seed, seedless; pleasure, pain; middle, not middle; void, not void; the other, I, another’, surely wishes to roll up the sky like a hide, to climb it with his feet as by a stair, to see the track of fish in the water and of birds in the sky: ‘not this, not this’, ‘from whom words turn back’, ‘who truly knows?’ (Ṛgveda). How then is he known as ‘he is my Self’? They tell a story. A simple man was told by some people, on account of some fault, ‘shame on you, you are no man’. To be assured that he was a man he went to someone and said ‘tell me, sir, who I am’. The other, seeing his simplicity, said ‘I will teach you by steps’, denied that he was a thing that does not move and so on, said ‘you are not a non-man’, and stopped. The simple man said: ‘you set out to teach me and have fallen silent; why do you not teach me?’ Your words are like his. One who does not grasp that he is a man when told ‘you are not a non-man’, how will he grasp it when told ‘you are a man’? Therefore the way of awakening to the Self is the teaching just as scripture gives it, and no other: what fire is to burn cannot be burnt by anything else. So scripture, setting out to teach the nature of the Self, says ‘not this, not this’, as in the denial of being a non-man, and stops; and it teaches ‘without inside, without outside’, ‘this Self is Brahman, the experiencer of all’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.5.19), ‘you are that’ (Chāndogya 6.8–16), ‘where all has become his very Self, by what should he see whom?’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.14). As long as a man does not know this Self in this way, he takes the adjunct, marked by the outer non-eternal seeing, for himself, through ignorance thinks the properties of the adjunct his own, and transmigrates under the power of ignorance, desire and action, returning again and again among gods, animals and men, from Brahmā down to a clump of grass. In what states he lives so, in an unbroken succession of births and deaths like the current of a river, the śruti now shows, to produce dispassion.

Śaṅkara: this one, who has ignorance, desire and action and takes them for his own, having performed sacrifice and other rites, comes from that world by the way of smoke and the rest, becomes food, and is offered in the fire that is man. In that man the transmigrating self, through the juices of the body in their order, first becomes an embryo in the form of seed. This seed is the vigour, the essence of the body, produced from all the limbs, the parts, of the lump that is made of food; being the man's own self it is called ‘a self’, and he bears that self, become an embryo as seed, in himself, in his own body. When his wife is in season he pours it into the woman, the fire that is woman, and then the father begets it. This going out from its place at the time the seed is poured is the first birth of this transmigrating self, the first state to become manifest.

words.meaning: the state of being her own self

grammar.en: past passive participle m. acc. sg.

translations.text: It becomes one with the woman's own self, just like a limb of her own. Therefore it does not hurt her. She nourishes this self of his (her husband's) that has come into her.

notes: Śaṅkara: the seed poured into the woman becomes not other than her self, as it was not other than the father's, just like her own limb, a breast or the like. For that reason the embryo does not hurt the mother, as a boil would. Knowing that this self of her husband has entered here, into her own belly, the pregnant woman makes it grow and guards it, avoiding food and the like that are harmful to the embryo and using what is helpful.

sanskrit.deva:
सा भावयित्री भावयितव्या भवति ।
तं स्त्री गर्भं बिभर्ति ।
सोऽग्र एव कुमारं जन्मनोऽग्रेऽधि भावयति ।
स यत्कुमारं जन्मनोऽग्रेऽधि भावयत्यात्मानमेव तद्भावयत्येषां लोकानां सन्तत्यै ।
एवं सन्तता हीमे लोकाः ।
तदस्य द्वितीयं जन्म ॥ ३ ॥

padaccheda.deva: सा भावयित्री भावयितव्या भवति तम् स्त्री गर्भम् बिभर्ति सः अग्रे एव कुमारम् जन्मनः अग्रे अधि भावयति सः यत् कुमारम् जन्मनः अग्रे अधि भावयति आत्मानम् एव तत् भावयति एषाम् लोकानाम् सन्तत्यै एवम् सन्तताः हि इमे लोकाः तत् अस्य द्वितीयम् जन्म

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. pl.

translations.text: She, the nourisher, is to be nourished (by her husband). The woman bears him as an embryo. He (the father) nourishes the child at the very first, just after its birth. In that he nourishes the child just after its birth, he nourishes his own self, for the continuance of these worlds; for thus are these worlds continued. That is its second birth.

notes: Śaṅkara: she who nourishes her husband's self, become an embryo, is to be nourished and protected by her husband; for in the world no one is bound to another without help given and returned. The woman bears the embryo, in the manner already told, before the birth. The father nourishes the child at the very first, as soon as it is born (agra eva), after the birth (janmano 'dhi), with the birth rite and the rest. In so doing he nourishes his own self, for it is the father's self that is born in the form of the son: ‘the husband enters the wife’ (Harivaṃśa). Why does he beget himself as a son and nourish him? For the continuance of these worlds, that they may not be cut off; they would be cut off if no one begot sons and did the rest. Because these worlds go on as a succession only through the unbroken doing of such acts, that is to be done for their continuance, not for liberation. The going out of this transmigrating self from the mother's belly as a child is the second birth, the second state to become manifest, counted from its form as seed.

sanskrit.deva:

स इतः प्रयन्नेव पुनर्जायते ।
तदस्य तृतीयं जन्म ॥ ४ ॥

words.meaning: having done what was to be done

translations.text: This self of his (the son) is put in his place for the meritorious rites. Then this other self of his (the father), having done what he had to do and advanced in age, departs. Just as he departs from here he is born again. That is his third birth.

notes: Śaṅkara: the father's self that is the son is put in the father's place to perform the rites taught by scripture, to do what the father had to do; as in the rite of handing over in the Vājasaneyaka the son, instructed by the father, accepts ‘I am Brahman, I am the sacrifice’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.5.17). Then, having laid his burden on the son, this other self of the son, the father, ‘having done what was to be done’, that is, freed from the three debts, old, dies. Even as he leaves this body he takes another, built up by his actions, like a caterpillar, and is born again; that which he is to reach after death is the third birth. It may be asked: the first birth told was that of the transmigrating self from the father as seed, and the second its birth from the mother as a child; when its third birth is to be told, how is the birth of the dead father called the third? There is no fault, because the oneness of father and son is meant. The son too, laying the burden on his own son, is born again just as he departs, like the father; the śruti holds that what is said of the one is said of the other, since father and son are one self.
The e-text reads karmebhyaḥ; it is set right here to karmabhyaḥ, as the bhāṣya reads.

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. sg.

translations.text: This was said by the seer: ‘While yet in the womb I came to know all the births of these gods. A hundred strongholds of iron held me down; then like a hawk I flew out with speed.’ Vāmadeva said this, in this way, while still lying in the womb.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: transmigrating thus, borne on the succession of births and deaths through the manifesting of the three states, the whole world has fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra; when a man somehow, in whatever state, comes to know the Self that the śruti teaches, at that very moment he is freed from all the bonds of saṃsāra and has done what was to be done.

Śaṅkara: that this is so was said by the seer too, in a mantra (Ṛgveda 4.27.1). ‘In the womb’: in the mother's womb itself; nu expresses reflection. Through the ripening of the meditation of many births, ‘I came to know all the births of these gods’, speech, fire and the rest. ‘A hundred’, many, ‘strongholds of iron’, that is, bodies that could not be broken, as if made of iron, ‘guarded me’, kept me down (adhaḥ) from getting out of the snare of saṃsāra. Then, like a hawk breaking through a net, ‘with speed’, with the strength that the knowledge of the Self gave, ‘I flew out’. See, the seer Vāmadeva said this while still lying in the womb.

padaccheda.deva: सः एवम् विद्वान् अस्मात् शरीर-भेदात् ऊर्ध्वम् उत्क्रम्य अमुष्मिन् स्वर्गे लोके सर्वान् कामान् आप्त्वा अमृतः समभवत् समभवत्

grammar.en: past active participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: He (Vāmadeva), knowing thus, on the break-up of this body, having risen up (out of saṃsāra, as the supreme Self), having obtained all desires, became immortal in that heavenly world (his own Self); he became immortal.

notes: Śaṅkara: the seer Vāmadeva, knowing the Self as described. ‘From the break-up of the body’: the body is imagined by ignorance, impenetrable as iron, a succession of bodies beset by hundreds of evils, birth, death and the rest; its break-up is wrought by the strength born of taking the nectar of the knowledge of the supreme Self: that is, the destruction of the body that comes from crushing ignorance and the other causes that are the seed of its arising. ‘Up’: being the supreme Self, he rose out of the lower state, saṃsāra, and reached the stainless state of being the Self of all, lit up by knowledge. ‘In that’, as described, undecaying, deathless, immortal, fearless, all-knowing, without before or after, without inside or outside, of the one savour of the nectar of consciousness, he went out like a lamp; ‘in the heavenly world’, in his own Self, in his own nature, he became immortal. ‘Having obtained all desires’: earlier, while still living, by the knowledge of the Self, as one whose desires are all attained. The repetition shows the end of the teaching of the knowledge of the Self, with its fruit and its example.
The e-text reads ūrdhvam utkramya, kept here; Śaṅkara glosses ūrdhvaḥ, and the Advaita Śāradā text reads ūrdhva utkramya.
